subtitle: What network graphics protocols need to handle for real interactive systems.

tldr.problem: Early network graphics protocol proposals are too narrowly focused on drawing primitives and do not account for interactive features like attention handling, picture structure, and user input devices.
tldr.mechanism: A complete graphics protocol must support multiple display types (storage tubes and refresh displays), various input devices (light pen, tablet, mouse), and a multilevel software stack from low-level commands through high-level application programming interfaces.
tldr.outcome: By considering hardware diversity and user interaction needs upfront, protocols can support everything from simple graphical terminals to sophisticated interactive applications.

facts.label: Input devices
facts.value: Light pen, tablet, mouse, joystick, keyboard

today: RFC 192 is a position paper from July 1971 arguing for comprehensive graphics protocol design. It influenced thinking about graphics systems but was not itself a protocol specification.

sections.title: Why Current Proposals Are Incomplete
sections.content: RFC 192 argues that network graphics protocol proposals at the time lack general enough mechanisms. Interactive graphics systems need to handle attention handling (responding to user input), picture structure (organizing complex drawings), and higher-level interactive graphics processes beyond simple drawing commands. The author observes that most industrial, academic and government applications using graphics terminals fall into three categories: roughly 75 percent need simple storage-tube displays (which draw once and hold the image indefinitely), 15-20 percent need refresh displays with simple animation, and the remainder need high-performance real-time picture processing. A protocol that accommodates this range requires more than just draw commands.
sections.eli5: When you design a system for drawing pictures over the network, you have to think about what happens when someone clicks the mouse, not just how to draw a line.

sections.title: A Multilevel Architecture
sections.content: The author proposes a multilevel modular approach with five layers: (1) basic system level providing low-level terminal commands for assembly language programmers, (2) high-level programming language support for interactive graphics, (3) picture editors or drawing systems, (4) data management support for application data linked to pictures, and (5) application programming itself. This philosophy lets inexperienced programmers use powerful, problem-oriented tools while experienced developers work at lower levels. Each level interfaces with surrounding levels, and designing them roughly in parallel allows experience from each to inform the others before they are finalized.
sections.eli5: Build the system in layers: bottom layer is raw commands, top layers are nicer tools that beginners can use. Each layer learns from the next to do its job better.

sections.title: Handling Different Display Types and Input Devices
sections.content: Storage tube displays can show many details without flicker and cost under 20,000 dollars, but cannot be selectively erased and can be slow if frequent redrawing is needed. Refresh displays cost from 10,000 to hundreds of thousands of dollars, repaint at 20-60 Hz, and allow smooth motion and selective erasure. A network protocol must work with both types. Input devices beyond the keyboard include the light pen, tablet, and mouse, allowing users to point at and select objects on the display. A graphics protocol must abstract these hardware differences so applications work with multiple display and input combinations, while letting new terminal types and devices be added without changing all applications.
sections.eli5: Screens are different: some keep a picture forever, some flicker if you are slow. Pointers work different ways. The protocol should let any program work with any screen-and-pointer combo.
